title-group.article-title: Tepotinib-induced interstitial lung disease in a patient with adenosquamous lung carcinoma

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: We report a case of drug-induced lung injury in an 88-year-old man with non-small cell lung cancer harboring an MET exon 14 skipping mutation. The patient developed dyspnea and new ground-glass opacities shortly after the initiation of tepotinib, an oral MET-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (MET-TKI). Clinical findings and laboratory data supported the diagnosis of tepotinib-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD). High-dose corticosteroid therapy led to improvement, and the patient was discharged. This case underscores the potential of early onset ILD with tepotinib, especially in patients with possible pre-existing ILD. Close monitoring and early intervention are essential, and further studies are needed to clarify the risk factors for MET-TKI-induced ILD.

sec.p: Keywords: MET-TKI, Tepotinib, ILD, Lung cancer
Received 2025 Jun 20; Revised 2025 Sep 28; Accepted 2025 Dec 26; Collection date 2026.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: MET exon 14 skipping mutations are found in 3–4 % of non-small cell lung cancers and are associated with a poor prognosis [1,2]. MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors (MET-TKIs) are small-molecule compounds that inhibit MET-mediated signaling and tumor growth by competitively binding to the ATP-binding site of MET tyrosine kinase [3]. Recently, three MET-TKIs (tepotinib, capmatinib, and gumarontinib) were developed to target MET exon 14 skipping mutations, demonstrating high response rates and favorable progression-free survival [[4], [5], [6]]. Various adverse reactions to MET-TKIs have been reported, including limb edema, nausea, diarrhea, renal dysfunction, hepatic dysfunction, and hypoalbuminemia. Cases of drug-induced lung injury associated with MET-TKI use have also been documented [7].

However, the frequency, timing, imaging characteristics, and risk factors of MET-TKI-induced lung injury remain poorly understood. We herein report a case of drug-induced lung injury that developed shortly after the initiation of tepotinib treatment.

sec.title: Case report
sec.p: The patient was an 88-year-old man with a 24-year history of smoking 30 cigarettes per day, along with comorbidities, including hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a history of traumatic liver injury. In February X–2, he underwent thoracoscopic resection of the right lower lobe at our hospital's Department of Respiratory Surgery for 15mm-sized mass. The patient was subsequently diagnosed with adenosquamous carcinoma of the lung, staged as pT1bN0M0 and pStage IA2. The patient was followed-up without any additional treatment.

In early March of year X, the patient developed right-sided chest pain. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a soft-tissue mass extending from the right chest wall to the diaphragm, osteolytic changes involving the right seventh through ninth ribs, and an infiltrative opacity in the right middle lobe. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/CT (FDG PET/CT) showed intense uptake in these newly identified lesions, consistent with postoperative recurrence. Consequently, palliative radiotherapy (40 Gy in 15 fractions) was administered to alleviate chest pain.

A MET exon 14 skipping mutation was identified by the AmoyDx® multi-gene PCR panel for lung cancer, performed on the surgical specimen obtained on February X-2. Given his performance status of 1, tepotinib was initiated at a dose of 500 mg on April 26, year X.
On April 27, the patient developed progressive dyspnea and presented to our outpatient clinic on May 1. He was admitted due to hypoxemia.

On admission, his vital signs were as follows: blood pressure, 166/86 mmHg; body temperature, 36.4 °C; respiratory rate, 24 breaths per minute; and percutaneous oxygen saturation (SpO2), 88 % on room air.
A physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds and fine crackles in the right and left lower lung fields, respectively. The other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory findings revealed the following: lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), 255 U/L (normal <222 U/L); C-reactive protein (CRP), 8.08 mg/dL (normal <0.5 mg/dL); and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), 65.2 pg/mL (normal <18.4 pg/mL) (Table 1). Krebs von den lugen-6 (KL-6) and surfactant protein D (SP-D)—biomarkers of alveolar epithelial injury—were 268 U/mL (normal <500 U/mL) and 584 ng/mL (normal <100 ng/mL), respectively (Table 1). No autoantibodies were elevated, and the patient did not fulfill the criteria for connective tissue diseases. The patient's procalcitonin and (1 → 3)-β-D-glucan levels were normal, a cytomegalovirus antigenemia assay (C7-HRP) was negative, and a SARS-CoV-2 quantitative antigen test was negative (Table 1).

sec.p: A chest radiograph taken on April 26, prior to tepotinib initiation, showed infiltrative shadows in the right lower lung field (Fig. 1a). A follow-up radiograph on April 30 showed improvement in these shadows, however, new ground-glass opacities developed throughout the left lung field (Fig. 1b).

caption.p: (a) A chest X-ray taken on April 26, prior to the administration of tepotinib, showed infiltrative shadows in the right lower lung field. (b) A chest X-ray taken on April 30, after the initiation of tepotinib, showed improvement in the infiltrative shadows in the right lower lung field; however, new ground-glass opacities appeared throughout the entire left lung field. (c) A chest X-ray taken on May 10, after the initiation of corticosteroid therapy, showed improvement in the ground-glass opacities in the left lung field.

sec.p: Chest CT performed on April 1, prior to tepotinib treatment, showed right pleural effusion, an infiltrative shadow in the right middle lobe, osteolysis of the right 7th rib, and mild reticulation at the left lung base —findings suggestive of pre-existing interstitial lung disease (ILD)—while emphysematous changes were minimal despite his smoking history (Fig. 2a–c). Repeat CT on April 30 showed an unchanged pleural effusion volume and improvement in the infiltrative shadow; however, new non-segmental ground-glass opacities appeared in the left upper and lower lobes, sparing the subpleural areas (Fig. 2d–f).

caption.p: (a–c) High-resolution chest tomography (HRCT) image taken on April 1, before the administration of tepotinib, showed a right pleural effusion, an infiltrative shadow in the right middle lobe, osteolysis of the right seventh rib, and a mild reticular shadow in the left lung base, raising suspicion of pre-existing interstitial lung disease. (d–f) HRCT taken on May 1, after the initiation of tepotinib, showed no change in the volume of the right pleural effusion; however, the infiltrative shadow in the right middle lobe, which was suspected to represent a lung cancer lesion, had improved. However, new non-segmental ground-glass opacities appeared in the left upper and lower lobes, sparing the subpleural regions. (g–i) HRCT taken on May 10, after the initiation of corticosteroid therapy, showed improvement in the ground-glass opacities in the left upper and lower lobe.

sec.p: Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) were considered but not performed because the patient required 5 L/min of oxygen and there was concern that the procedure would exacerbate his hypoxia.

A clinical diagnosis of tepotinib-induced lung injury was made based on the acute onset of ground-glass opacities after the initiation of tepotinib, elevated SP-D, the absence of infectious findings, and lack of echocardiographic or other evidence of heart failure.

The treatment consisted of a steroid half-pulse regimen with methylprednisolone (500 mg) for 3 days starting on April 30, followed by tapering (Fig. 3). As his oxygen needs declined, chest radiography and CT on May 10 (Fig. 1, Fig. 2i) showed improvement and his laboratory values normalized. He was discharged on May 14, year X.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Currently, three MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors (MET-TKIs), tepotinib, capmatinib, and gumarontinib, are approved in Japan for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with MET exon 14 skipping mutations. The incidence of ILD reported in global Phase II trials was 3.8 % (5/130 patients) in the VISION trial for tepotinib [8]; 6.2 % (6/97 patients) in the GEOMETRY mono-1 trial for capmatinib [9]; and 1.2 % (1/84 patients) in the GLORY trial for gumarontinib [10]. The median time to the onset of ILD was 54 days (range: 21–35 days) for tepotinib [8], 48.5 days (range: 5–451 days) for capmatinib [9], and 28 days for gumarontinib in the only case [10].

A review of the relevant literature identified four published case reports of capmatinib-induced ILD and three reports related to tepotinib, including the present case [[11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]]. Among these, two patients had preexisting ILD, one of whom was reported in an autopsy case. There are only a few exceptional case reports describing the use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) targeting driver gene mutations, such as EGFR mutations, in patients with NSCLC complicated by ILD [17]. In routine clinical practice, EGFR-TKIs are generally contraindicated in such patients [17]. However, the safety of MET-TKIs in NSCLC patients with ILD remains unclear, especially in cases with mild findings, such as reticular shadows, as observed in the present case, making treatment decisions more challenging.

Although the package inserts for tepotinib, capmatinib, and gumarontinib advise caution in patients with ILD, they do not list ILD as a contraindication [[18], [19], [20]]. Among the seven previously reported cases of MET-TKI-induced ILD, two involved patients with preexisting ILD, suggesting that underlying ILD may be a risk factor for this adverse event. Therefore, caution should be exercised when initiating MET-TKI therapy in such cases.

The median time to the onset of ILD in international Phase II trials ranged from 28 to 54 days [[8], [9], [10]]. In the seven case reports, ILD most commonly developed 1–2 months after the initiation of treatment (Table 2). However, two patients developed ILD within the first week, indicating that an early onset was possible. These findings suggest that close monitoring, including inpatient observation, may be warranted, particularly during the early phase of treatment.

sec.p: The mortality rate of MET-TKI-induced lung injury in clinical trials remains unknown owing to the limited number of reported cases. Although the response to corticosteroid therapy is generally considered favorable, one of the seven previously reported patients with pre-existing ILD died despite receiving high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy (Table 2). These findings suggest that pre-existing ILD may not only predispose patients to MET-TKI-induced lung injury but may also serve as a poor prognostic factor for its outcome.

Of the four patients with capmatinib-induced ILD, three were subsequently switched to tepotinib and experienced favorable outcomes. In contrast, no cases have been reported in which patients were switched to capmatinib following tepotinib-induced ILD. These observations suggested that tepotinib may pose a lower risk of drug-induced ILD than capmatinib. Regarding gumarontinib, comparisons remain limited owing to its recent approval and relatively low use. Further large-scale clinical studies are necessary to determine the risk of ILD associated with each of the three MET-TKIs.

There are several limitations in this case report. First, bronchoscopy—including BAL and transbronchial lung biopsy—was not performed when diagnosing tepotinib-induced ILD. Second, this is a single-patient report, which limits the generalizability of the findings.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We report a case of drug-induced lung injury caused by tepotinib. The onset of symptoms occurred shortly after the initiation of treatment, and the clinical course progressed relatively rapidly, indicating the need for careful monitoring. As case reports remain scarce, the further accumulation of clinical experience is required.
